analysis.one_liner: Requires outside election spenders to disclose the donors behind their campaign ads.
analysis.headline: A campaign-disclosure bill with 165 House cosponsors was referred to two committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE 2012 Act would have forced any corporation, union, or tax-exempt group that spends more than $10,000 on politics to report that spending to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, along with the names of anyone who gave them $10,000 or more. TV and radio ads would have had to name the biggest funders on screen or on air, CEOs would have to appear in ads saying their company approves the message, shareholders and members would have been told about political spending in their organizations' reports, and registered lobbyists would have had to report their own election spending. It never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would have learned who was paying for political ads attacking or supporting candidates. Shareholders, union members, and donors, who would have been told how their own organizations spent money on elections [S3]. The FEC and election officials, who would have gotten a faster, fuller record of outside spending [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Any covered organization - a corporation, union, tax-exempt group, or political organization - spending more than $10,000 a year on campaign ads or transfers would have to file a sworn statement with the FEC within 24 hours, naming each person who gave $10,000 or more toward that spending [S3].
TV ads paid for with covered spending would have to show a list of the top five funders for at least six seconds, and radio ads the top two, so viewers could see who was behind the message [S3].
Ads would have to end with a named officer - a company's CEO, for example - saying 'I approve this message,' extending the stand-by-your-ad rule to outside groups [S3].
Organizations that report to shareholders, members, or donors would have to include their political spending in those reports, and post a link to their FEC filings on their homepages [S3].
Registered lobbyists would have to report independent expenditures and electioneering communications of $1,000 or more, with the candidate supported or opposed [S2].

The bill broadened the legal definition of an 'independent expenditure' to include communications that are the functional equivalent of telling people to vote for or against a candidate, closing a loophole that let groups avoid disclosure [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, and especially tax-exempt 'dark money' groups making political spending, who would bear compliance costs and lose the anonymity of their largest donors. Some donors who feared retaliation for being publicly linked to a candidate might have given less or through harder-to-trace routes.

drawbacks.text: The $10,000 disclosure threshold and the demand for donor names could deter some people from giving to advocacy groups at all, on the theory that public lists of political donors invite harassment - a concern the bill's own exception for donors who restrict their money to non-political use implicitly acknowledges [S3].

The new 'functional equivalent of express advocacy' standard asks regulators to judge what a communication 'can be interpreted by a reasonable person' to mean, which would draw difficult line-drawing between campaign ads and genuine issue advocacy and invite legal challenge [S2].
Twenty-four-hour reporting, CEO appearances in ads, top-funder crawls, and new shareholder and lobbyist reports would impose real compliance costs on covered organizations large and small [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: voters would know who financed the ads trying to influence their votes, and members and shareholders would see how their own organizations spend politically. The costs are genuine but narrower - compliance burdens and a possible chilling of some donors who fear publicity. On balance the bill trades donor anonymity for public information, and the design (thresholds, exceptions for ordinary business and restricted funds) shows an attempt to target big political spending rather than all group activity [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees without a hearing or vote, its sponsor filed a petition to force it to the floor, and the petition never got the signatures needed - so the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 9, 2012 and referred to the House Administration Committee and the Judiciary Committee; neither acted on it [S1].
Sixteen days after introduction it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution, a step from which it never emerged [S5].

On July 12, 2012, sponsor Rep. Van Hollen filed a discharge petition - a device requiring signatures from a majority of the House, 218 members, to pull a bill out of committee and onto the floor [S5].
No action followed the petition filing; the bill received no committee vote and no floor vote during the 112th Congress [S5].
All 165 cosponsors were Democrats, and the House was controlled by Republicans during this period [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Outside spending groups - tax-exempt nonprofits, super PACs, and their corporate backers - kept the ability to run campaign ads without naming their major donors, and the incumbent committee chairs kept control over what reached the floor.

for.name: Rep. Chris Van Hollen
for.role: Sponsor; filed discharge petition No. 112-4 to force the bill to the floor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, and filed a discharge petition on July 12, 2012 to try to pull it out of committee and onto the House floor.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including House Democratic leaders Steny Hoyer and James Clyburn as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House schedule
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or allowed it to advance after the discharge petition was filed.

against.name: House committee chairs

sides.party_line_note: All 165 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans; the bill never came to a vote in the Republican-controlled House [S4].

industries.note: These groups would have had to file within 24 hours after spending $10,000 or more on campaigns and name every donor who gave $10,000 or more, ending the anonymity that makes them the main vehicle for undisclosed election spending [S3]. Their interest in keeping donor identities secret runs directly against the bill's purpose of informing voters.

industries.industry: Super PACs and corporate-funded outside spenders
industries.note: Their ads would have had to carry the names of top funders on screen and a statement from a company officer, and transfers passed through chains of groups to hide the original source would have been traced and reported [S3].

Unions are covered organizations under the bill, so they would face the same spending reports, donor disclosure, and ad disclaimers as corporations [S3]. Unions represent members who would gain the shareholder-style disclosure, but as political spenders they shared the industry interest in avoiding it.
Lobbyists would have had to report their own independent expenditures and electioneering communications of $1,000 or more in semiannual filings, adding to existing lobbying reports [S2].
